units: a charger in use grows warm
the current runs through a copper winding inside the device
every conducting material resists the passage of the current
this resistance turns part of the energy into heat
a greater demand for power increases the share that is lost
makers provide vents, metal contact parts and sometimes a cooling fan
a device that gets too hot slows its own pace
a soft object placed under a computer blocks the air openings
text: Put your hand on a charger you have left plugged in. It feels warm, and there is nothing odd in that. Inside the casing, current runs along thin wires and round a copper winding. No conductor lets electricity through for free; it pushes back, and that pushing back turns a slice of the energy into heat. The more power the device draws, the bigger the slice grows. Designers know as much, so they cut vents into the shell, press metal plates against the busiest components, or tuck in a tiny fan. When the heat has nowhere to go, the circuits throttle themselves to stay safe, and the machine turns sluggish. That is why a cushion slipped under a laptop smothers it: the slots close up, the air sits still, the temperature climbs. Pull the plug, give the thing room to breathe, and it will settle down again.

units: dead tablets were piling up in a repair workshop
the devices showed no sign of life at all
the explanation put forward blamed the battery
the head of the workshop doubted that diagnosis
taking one apart revealed a cracked metal joint beneath the charging socket
a light knock was enough to break it
the team built a cradle that holds the board still while the joint is redone
the repair became cheap to carry out
the workshop displays its repair notes publicly
text: At the far end of a shopping arcade, a repair workshop had been stacking up silent tablets for weeks. The verdict never varied: black screen, no response at all, a battery said to be finished. The senior repairer would not swallow so tidy and convenient a story. He opened one machine, then a second, and found beneath the charging socket a cracked metal joint, far too fine to spot without a lens. A modest knock was all it took to split it. Rather than swap out whole boards, the team shaped a cradle that grips the board firmly while a hot iron rebuilds the failed point. Putting a tablet right now costs next to nothing, and owners walk out with a machine that has woken up. Repair notes hang on a board beside the counter, so that people stop throwing away what a bead of solder would bring back.

units: two distinct ways exist to take apart an old playback device
the first means removing the screws one at a time
the first calls for noting where the parts sit on a drawing
the second means forcing the shell open with a flat tool
the second usually damages a catch
the careful method needs an adjustable lamp and a clear bench
the bundles of wire make the difference between the two approaches plain
the text recommends the careful method
putting it back together follows the reverse order
text: Before you loosen a single nut, choose your road, for an old player can be opened in two ways. The first belongs to patience: the screws come out one at a time, each dropped into a shallow saucer, each place marked on a sketch. The second belongs to nerve: a flat blade prises the lid up, a moment is saved, and a catch is lost. Patience asks for a lamp on a bendable arm and a bench swept bare; nerve asks for nothing but a firm wrist. Yet once the wiring shows itself, a thin garland pressed against the floor of the frame, the gap between them opens wide: the careful hand knows where every ribbon returns, while the hasty one pulls blind and tears. Take the first road, then. Build the thing back up in reverse order, and let the drawer spring settle back before the lid goes down.

units: the sorting line described has three complementary pieces of equipment
light sensors read the reflection to identify what the packaging is made of
jets of compressed air push aside the unwanted items
this ejection happens without anything touching the objects
belts running at unequal speeds spread the flow and stop items piling up
the manager reckons upkeep matters more than the software
a dirty nozzle sends the ejected pieces off course
a slack belt upsets the rhythm of the line
a dusty sensor takes glass for clear plastic
a worker inspects the installation regularly to clean it
text: The shed hums with a steady drone, and the guided tour opens in front of the first sorting line. Three pieces of kit work in concert here. The first is a curtain of optical sensors that measures how each pack throws light back and works out what it is made of. The second is a rail of compressed air nozzles, firing to the thousandth of a second to fling out unwanted pieces without ever touching them. The third is a run of belts whose gears turn at differing speeds, spreading the flow so that nothing rides on anything else. The operator presses a point visitors tend to miss: reliability rests less on the software than on upkeep. A clogged nozzle skews the throw; a slack belt shifts the timing; a dusty sensor takes glass for clear plastic. So a worker walks the line at set intervals, cloth in hand.

units: the assembly described follows a fixed sequence of operations
a cut sheet of metal is given its final shape under a press
a sheathed metal wire is wound around a central core
the ends of that winding are stripped of their sheath
a magnetic part sits in the outer ring and is locked by a collar
the shaft is oiled before it is fitted
the turning of the shaft is checked with no load
the wires of the winding are fixed with solder onto conducting pads
the shell closes on a seal that keeps out the dust
the finished object undergoes a load test in a booth
text: Watch an assembly line for a while and a strict order emerges, followed from the first movement to the last. A cut steel plate reaches a turning table, where a press stamps the shape of the housing into it. Winding comes next: lacquered copper wire runs round a core and builds an even coil, whose ends will later be stripped bare. A permanent magnet then drops into the outer ring and is held there by a collar. The shaft is offered up, oiled, driven home, and its turn is checked with no load on it. Once that has passed, the ends of the coil meet two conducting pads, where a machine lays down a bead of solder. The casing is closed last of all, on a soft seal that keeps the dust outside. The whole thing then goes off to the test booth, where a measured load proves how well it holds.

units: putting a household appliance back into working order has become difficult
shells are now glued together rather than screwed
the screw heads used are not sold in ordinary shops
spare parts stop being sold soon after a model goes out
the buyer gives up on repair and buys a replacement product
objects that half an hour would mend are thrown away
independent shops disappear for want of custom
technical skills are lost when those shops close
some makers show that a lid you can lift adds nothing to the bulk
the text calls for standard screws, wiring diagrams to hand and parts in stock
text: Mending a household appliance was once routine work; today it counts as a feat. The reasons are plain enough. Makers have glued the shells together instead of screwing them, settled on screw heads no ordinary shop stocks, and stopped selling spare parts a short while after a model goes out. Each of those decisions has a measurable effect. The owner gives up, buys a replacement, and something half an hour of work would have saved ends up in a skip. Independent shops close for want of custom, and the skill they carried fades with them. Slimness and sealing no longer excuse it: some makers prove that a lid you can lift adds nothing to the bulk. Asking for standard screws, a wiring diagram you can obtain and a lasting stock of parts is no fond wish for the past; it is what long use depends on.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman knew nothing of mechanical words when she started
she taught herself by taking broken toys apart
she runs a small shop set between two other businesses
her first difficulty came from the awkwardness her customers felt
the customers were afraid of getting it wrong as they described their trouble
she changed the way she receives the public
she opens the device in front of its owner and names each part as she points
customers come back having worked out the fault themselves
the shop is no longer short of custom
text: She says that at the start she muddled up a cog and a pulley, and that she taught herself by pulling old broken toys to bits. The mender of the neighbourhood now keeps a narrow shop, wedged between a launderette and a florist. Her trouble in the early days was not mechanical at all: it was how shy her customers were. Nobody dared describe a fault out loud, for fear of saying something daft. So she changed the way she takes people in. She sets the machine down on the counter, opens it up in front of its owner, and names each part aloud: here is the catch that sticks, here is the power socket, here is the gear that slips. Customers now leave having understood. A good many of them come back later with a fault they have pinned down themselves, and the shop is never empty now.

units: the two machines compared follow opposite designs
the first favours suction power and sturdiness
the first does well on thick textile floor coverings
the first makes a noise that drives the household away
the first leaves dirt in the corners
the second stands out for how well it finds its way about
the second pulls with less force and takes longer to finish the surface
the second avoids obstacles and slips under low furniture
the choice depends on the sort of floor and how cluttered the home is
both machines open and empty without a tool
text: Set side by side on the same shelf, two robot cleaners tell two opposite stories. The first backs sheer force: an eager motor, a wide brush, a generous bin, and a body that shrugs off knocks. It shines on deep rugs, but its racket drives the whole household out of the room, and its corner arm leaves crescents of dust in the angles. The second plays a finer game: careful navigation, a map you can trust, a return to base with no dithering. It pulls less hard and takes longer to cover the floor, yet it bumps into nothing and slips under low furniture. The verdict turns on the home: hard floors and tight furniture, and the second wins; deep pile and open rooms, and the first takes the lead. On one score they are equal: the bin tips out in a moment, and the lid lifts with no tool.

units: the writer reports on the restoration of a radio set found in the loft
the work falls into three separate tasks
the cabinet was sanded, glued at one corner and waxed
the inside was covered in a thick deposit
two wires had lost their covering
the connections were remade wire by wire
the needle of the dial no longer follows the turning knob
the writer supposes that a springy part is worn
the writer promises to write again once the set is working
text: You asked me how the radio from the loft was getting on, and I owe you an account of it at last. Three separate tasks have kept me busy. The cabinet came first: I sanded down the lifted veneer, glued a corner that had sprung open, replaced a missing beading, then rubbed in a wax that woke the grain of the wood again. The inside came second, and there my patience wavered: dust lay like a grey felt over every valve, and two wires had shed their covering. I remade the connections strand by strand, with fresh wire and a clean, bright joint. The third task holds me still: the needle on the dial refuses to follow the knob any longer, and I suspect a tired spring. When it is all ready at last, I shall set the thing by the window and write to tell you what the first voice says.

units: a specialist describes the updating of the internal software of a device
the device first checks that the file it has received is genuine
the procedure stops if that check fails
the new data is written into an area of memory apart from the one in use
this separation protects the device if the power is cut
the earlier version remains until the restart
a counter of attempts turns the start back to the old area if the writing fails
the user then notices only a slower start
the fingerprints of the two areas are compared after the switch
the space of the stale version is freed only after a session without fault
text: What actually happens when the internal software of a machine is brought up to date? The engineer we asked sets out the stages in order. First the device checks the signature of the file it has received; if that does not match, the whole procedure halts at once. The image is then written into a second area of memory, never over the one at work, so that a power cut can damage nothing. And the earlier version? It stays whole until the restart. And if the writing fails? A counter of attempts turns the start back to the old area, and the user notices no more than a slightly heavier start than usual. After the switch, a final check compares the fingerprints of the two areas. The machine frees the space of the stale version last of all, and only after a full session with nothing amiss.
